summary: To support internationalization and a more diverse Internet community, the RFC Series needs to allow non-ASCII characters. English remains the required language, but future RFCs will be encoded in UTF-8. This informational document describes how non-ASCII characters are used in RFCs.

plainLanguage.summary: RFCs used to use only basic English letters. Now they can include characters from other languages, such as in people's names. This explains the rules for that.

questions: how are non-latin author names written in rfcs
subtitle: The rules for when and how RFCs may use characters beyond plain ASCII.

tldr.problem: RFCs were ASCII-only, which hinders readable, internationalized content such as author names and examples of internationalized protocols.
tldr.mechanism: RFCs switch to UTF-8 as the default encoding and allow non-ASCII characters only where necessary, with ASCII alternatives, Unicode code points in the U+ notation, and an ascii attribute in the XML.
tldr.outcome: Readability overrides use of non-ASCII text, and the RFC Editor may reject code points that do not render adequately. The document updates RFC 7322 and is itself updated by RFC 9920.

facts.label: Code point notation
facts.value: U+ followed by the hex value, e.g. U+2206

today: RFC 7997 is an Informational document and is updated by RFC 9920. It updates RFC 7322, and its details were expected to change as the publication toolsets were completed.

sections.title: From ASCII to UTF-8
sections.content:
For much of its history the RFC Series used ASCII (RFC 20). That was sensible: the language is English, and ASCII is the lowest common denominator that makes cross-platform viewing trivial. But the growing need for readable, internationalized content means it is time to allow non-ASCII characters where necessary.

RFCs will therefore support UTF-8 as the default encoding and a broad range of Unicode characters. The RFC Editor may reject any code point that does not render adequately across all formats or in enough rendering engines using the v3 tooling. Non-ASCII use should be limited to where it is necessary. This document updates the RFC Style Guide (RFC 7322), and its details were expected to change with experience.
sections.plainLanguage: RFCs only used simple keyboard letters because every computer could show them. Now other letters are allowed, but only when they are really needed.

sections.title: The Two Basic Requirements
sections.content:
Two requirements shape all the guidance. First, searches against RFC indexes and database tables must return expected results and support appropriate Unicode string matching. Second, RFCs must display correctly across a wide range of readers and browsers. People whose systems lack the needed fonts must still be able to read the publication formats and the XML well enough to understand and implement the document.

If non-ASCII characters hurt readability, the RFC Editor will request alternate text. For text made entirely of non-ASCII words, the RFC Editor may ask reviewers to verify the meaning, spelling, characters and grammar. Because the language of the Series is English, spelling follows the primary entry in the Merriam-Webster dictionary by default.
sections.plainLanguage: Two promises: you must be able to search for things, and everyone must be able to read the page even if their computer lacks a special font.

sections.title: Names, Addresses and Citations
sections.content:
Person names: when a name uses a script outside the Unicode Latin blocks, an author-provided, ASCII-only identifier appears right after it in parentheses. This applies in the header, the Acknowledgements and the references.

Company names: valid Unicode is required, and names with characters outside the Latin and Latin Extended scripts need an author-provided ASCII-only identifier to help searching and indexing.

References: the entry must be in English, with every subfield available in ASCII. Non-ASCII characters may be added at the author's discretion, and the RFC Editor may ask a third party to review them.

Keywords and citation tags must contain only ASCII. Addresses: authors may use their official postal address, and a valid non-ASCII email address, without extra escapes.
sections.plainLanguage: If a name is written in another alphabet, a plain-letter version goes right next to it in brackets so everyone can read and search for it.

sections.title: Non-ASCII Characters in the Text
sections.content:
When a non-ASCII character is needed for correct protocol operation and understanding, its Unicode code point must be given in the text, in the U+ notation. Showing the actual UTF-8 character is encouraged so the reader can see it if their device can render it, and so is giving the Unicode character name in capital letters, such as INCREMENT.

The RFC lists six acceptable ways to identify a character. For example, the Delta character can be written as the U+2206 character with its glyph, with its name INCREMENT, or both. Which form is best depends on context, and all are acceptable. Where non-ASCII characters are only part of an example and not required for protocol operation, escaping is not required.

Tables follow the same rules, and authors may use two tables if that is clearer. In code components the RFC Editor encourages U+ notation except where the programming language's own rules apply, and fixed-width fonts are expected. Authors should not expect Unicode normalization forms to be preserved, so if a form is expected, the text should say so.
sections.plainLanguage: When a strange character matters, the RFC says its secret number, like a seat number for each character, and may show the character and its name too.

sections.title: XML Markup and Security
sections.content:
To make it easy for code to find the ASCII alternatives, authors must include an ascii attribute in their XML markup wherever an ASCII alternative is required, as described in RFC 7991.

The internationalization section says that clear, consistent non-ASCII use will help describe internationalized protocols and recognize the diversity of authors, but that readability overrides the use of non-ASCII characters. The security section is one sentence: valid Unicode that matches the expected text must be verified, to preserve expected behavior and protocol information.
sections.plainLanguage: The source file has a special label that holds the plain-letter version, and the checkers make sure the special characters are the right ones.

viz.caption: WHERE ASCII ALTERNATIVES ARE REQUIRED OR ALLOWED (RFC 7997)

items.title: Person names
items.text: Non-Latin scripts get an ASCII-only identifier in parentheses.

items.title: Company names
items.text: Valid Unicode required; ASCII identifier for non-Latin scripts.

items.title: Addresses
items.text: Official postal and valid email addresses need no escapes.
